report:
# Does Arthroscopy Help Knee Osteoarthritis? — No, the Evidence Says

Your instinct is correct: high-quality evidence consistently shows arthroscopic knee surgery does **not** meaningfully help osteoarthritis.

**Key evidence:**

The most rigorous test came from Moseley et al.'s landmark placebo-controlled trial in the *New England Journal of Medicine* (2002), which randomized patients to arthroscopic debridement, lavage, or sham surgery. At no point over two years did the arthroscopy groups report less pain or better function than the placebo group (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259). A follow-up randomized trial by Kirkley et al. (NEJM, 2008) compared arthroscopic surgery plus physical/medical therapy versus physical/medical therapy alone in moderate-to-severe OA, again finding no significant benefit from surgery (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0708333).

The **Cochrane Collaboration**, the gold standard for systematic evidence synthesis, updated its review in 2022, analyzing 16 randomized/quasi-randomized trials. It concluded that arthroscopic surgery provides "little or no clinically important benefit" for people with degenerative knee disease, including osteoarthritis and degenerative meniscal tears, compared with placebo or non-surgical care (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease).

Based on this accumulated evidence, the UK's **NICE** guidelines now strongly recommend *against* arthroscopic knee washout/debridement for osteoarthritis (https://ebi.aomrc.org.uk/interventions/knee-arthroscopy-for-patients-with-osteoarthritis/).

**Bottom line:** Despite arthroscopy remaining common in practice, randomized controlled trials and Cochrane's systematic review confirm it offers no meaningful advantage over sham surgery or conservative treatment for knee osteoarthritis, and major clinical guidelines now advise against it.
